title: Data import
summary: Read the Larkhaven Bikes monthly station exports, which were written for people rather than R: skip a title line, declare missing-value codes and column types, find parsing problems, clean the names and numbers, read twelve files at once, see which column types a CSV file keeps and which an RDS file keeps, and type a small table by hand.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse) and library(janitor)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes readr
load janitor, for cleaning column names

steps.explain: readr, part of the tidyverse, reads text files such as CSV. janitor has tools for tidying messy data; this lesson uses one of them. Its message lists two statistics functions it replaces, which this lesson doesn't use.

steps.title: A first look: read_csv(), skip and na

runs.purpose: read January's station export as it is
runs.task: Read `data/exports/station-activity-2025-01.csv` with `read_csv()`, without any other arguments.

runs.purpose: read it again, skipping the title line
runs.task: Read the same file again, skipping its first line with `skip = 1`.

runs.purpose: read it again, with the codes the export uses for missing values
runs.task: Read it again with `skip = 1`, and tell `read_csv()` that empty cells, `n/a` and `-` mean a missing value: `na = c("", "n/a", "-")`.

steps.explain: The file's first line is a title, not column names, so the first read made one column named after the title, put each whole line in it, and warned about parsing issues. `skip = 1` skips the title: {n_rows} stations, with 10 named columns. In that read, `Avg Duration (min)` is text (`<chr>`), because the export writes a missing value as `n/a`, `-` or nothing. `na` lists the codes that mean missing; with them, the column is a number (`<dbl>`), with `NA` where a value is missing.

steps.title: Column types: col_types and problems()

runs.code:
jan <- read_csv(
  "data/exports/station-activity-2025-01.csv",
  skip = 1,
  na = c("", "n/a", "-"),
  col_types = cols(`Dock Faults` = col_integer())
)
alternatives: jan = read_csv('data/exports/station-activity-2025-01.csv', skip = 1, na = c('', 'n/a', '-'), col_types = cols(`Dock Faults` = 'i'))
runs.purpose: read January into `jan`, with `Dock Faults` as whole numbers
runs.task: Read the file into `jan` as in the last statement, adding `col_types = cols(`Dock Faults` = col_integer())` so that column is read as whole numbers.

runs.purpose: list the values that didn't fit their column's type
runs.task: List the parsing problems in `jan` with `problems()`.

steps.explain: Left to guess, `read_csv()` made `Dock Faults` text. `col_types` says what a column holds instead: `col_integer()` for whole numbers. One value isn't a whole number, so R warned, and `problems()` says where: in column 9, where it expected an integer, it found `2 (est.)`, someone's estimate. That cell is `NA` in `jan`; the others are whole numbers, or `NA` where the export left them missing. Names with spaces, such as `Dock Faults`, need backticks in code.

steps.title: Names and units: clean_names() and parse_number()

runs.code:
jan |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    avg_trip_distance = parse_number(avg_trip_distance),
    e_bike_share = parse_number(e_bike_share)
  )
alternatives: jan |> clean_names() |> mutate(e_bike_share = parse_number(e_bike_share), avg_trip_distance = parse_number(avg_trip_distance))
runs.purpose: give the columns names that are easy to type, and take the units out of two of them
runs.task: Clean `jan`'s column names with `clean_names()`, then turn `avg_trip_distance` and `e_bike_share` into numbers with `parse_number()` inside `mutate()`.

steps.explain: `clean_names()` rewrote every column name in snake case, lower case with words joined by underscores: `Avg Duration (min)` became `avg_duration_min`, which needs no backticks. `parse_number()` reads the number out of a piece of text and drops what's around it: `{first_distance}` became {first_distance_number} and `{first_share}` became {first_share_number}. A unit belongs in a column's name or its notes, not in every cell, where it stops the column being a number.

steps.title: Twelve files into one: read_csv() with id

runs.purpose: list the monthly export files in `files`
runs.task: List the files in `data/exports` and store their paths in `files`, with `list.files()` and `full.names = TRUE`.

runs.code:
activity <- read_csv(files, skip = 1, na = c("", "n/a", "-"), id = "file") |>
  clean_names()
alternatives: activity = clean_names(read_csv(files, skip = 1, na = c('', 'n/a', '-'), id = 'file'))
runs.purpose: read all twelve months into `activity`, recording each row's file
runs.task: Read every file in `files` into `activity` with one `read_csv()` call: `skip = 1`, the same `na`, and `id = "file"`. Then clean its names.

runs.purpose: total the trips started in each file, that is each month

steps.explain: `list.files()` found the 12 monthly exports. Given all their paths, `read_csv()` read them into one data frame of {n_activity} rows, which works because they share the same columns. `id = "file"` added a column saying which file each row came from, so the months stay apart: the stations started {january} trips in January and {july} in July.

steps.title: Saving as CSV: write_csv()

runs.purpose: read the CSV file back, and look at the type of `Dock Faults`

steps.explain: `write_csv()` saved `jan` as `jan.csv`, which is in the Files pane. A CSV file is plain text that any program can open, but it doesn't record column types. In `jan`, `Dock Faults` holds whole numbers (`<int>`), because you chose `col_integer()`. Read back, `read_csv()` guessed the types again, and its message lists `Dock Faults` under `dbl`: your choice is lost.

steps.title: Saving as RDS: write_rds()

runs.purpose: read the RDS file back, and look at the type of `Dock Faults` again

steps.explain: An RDS file stores an R object exactly, so `read_rds()` gave `jan` back as it was, with `Dock Faults` still `<int>`. Only R reads RDS files, though. Parquet, in lesson 22, keeps the types and can be read by many tools.

steps.title: Small data by hand: tribble()

runs.purpose: type a small table of the three depots and their mechanics into `depots`
runs.task: Make a data frame `depots` with `tribble()`: a column `depot` holding "Northgate", "Harbour" and "Eastfield", and a column `mechanics` holding 3, 2 and 3.

steps.explain: `tribble()` builds a small data frame from values you type, one row per line, with the column names first, each after a `~`. It suits lookup tables like this one: the scheme's three repair depots and how many mechanics each has. RStudio's formatter, Air, lines the columns up so the code reads like the table it makes. `tibble()` builds the same thing a column at a time.
